query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperature, the protective oxide films that normally form on the eutectic HEA are continuously disrupted by mechanical wear, leading to repeated exposure of fresh, unoxidized metal surfaces that corrode rapidly. This cyclic breakdown of the nascent oxide layers accelerates the overall degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure as produced by conventional casting.
generation.intervention: Introduce a pre-oxidation passivation treatment to create a more robust, adherent oxide layer before exposure to simultaneous wear and corrosion.
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (600–700°C) in an oxidizing atmosphere under sliding (tribocorrosion) conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The interphase boundaries where thin, nascent oxide films form and are subsequently disrupted.
generation.mechanism: Under high temperatures, each phase develops its own oxide film. However, due to differences in oxidation kinetics between the soft fcc and hard B2 phases, the interface oxide is inherently fragile. When mechanical wear acts on the surface, this film is repeatedly spalled off, exposing fresh metal that rapidly corrodes. The combined process yields accelerated degradation due to the synergy between wear-induced mechanical disruption and corrosive re-oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the untreated alloy will show an increased overall degradation with both higher abrasive wear (due to lack of lubrication by the oxide film) and more pronounced corrosion attack (due to continuous exposure of fresh metal). Introducing a stable passivating oxide layer should reduce the total degradation (both wear and corrosion) by inhibiting the cyclic film breakdown.
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic HEA without any pre-oxidation or passivating treatment.
generation.boundary: Sustained high temperatures (600–700°C), an oxidizing atmosphere, and applied sliding wear forces representative of relevant service conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in degradation from the pre-passivation treatment is uncertain due to limited characterization of high-temperature oxide film kinetics on such dual-phase materials.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the eutectic HEA samples: one set undergoes a controlled pre-oxidation passivation treatment to form a continuous oxide film, and the other set is left in the as-cast state. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature tribocorrosion tests (e.g., sliding wear in an oxidizing environment at 700°C) and measure weight loss, friction coefficients, and oxide layer integrity.
measurements: Weight loss over time
Surface morphology and oxide film continuity (via SEM/EDS)
Friction coefficient and wear track profile
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passivated samples do not exhibit at least a 10% reduction in overall degradation (both wear and corrosion metrics) compared to the untreated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-temperature corrosion is chemical deterioration of a material (typically a metal) as a result of heating. This non-galvanic form of corrosion can occur when a metal is subjected to a hot atmosphere containing oxygen, sulfur ("sulfidation"), or other compounds capable of oxidizing (or assisting the oxidation of) the material concerned. For example, materials used in aerospace, power generation, and even in car engines must resist sustained periods at high temperature, during which they may be exposed to an atmosphere containing the potentially highly-corrosive products of combustion. Some products of high-temperature corrosion can potentially be turned to the advantage of the engineer. The formation of oxides on stainless steels, for example, can provide a protective layer preventing further atmospheric attack, allowing for a material to be used for sustained periods at both room and high temperatures in hostile conditions. Such high-temperature corrosion products, in the form of compacted oxide layer glazes, prevent or reduce wear during high-temperature sliding contact of metallic (or metallic and ceramic) surfaces. Fretting wear is the repeated cyclical rubbing between two surfaces. Over a period of time fretting which will remove material from one or both surfaces in contact. It occurs typically in bearings, although most bearings have their surfaces hardened to resist the problem. Another problem occurs when cracks in either surface are created, known as fretting fatigue. It is the more serious of the two phenomena because it can lead to catastrophic failure of the bearing. An associated problem occurs when the small particles removed by wear are oxidized in air. The oxides are usually harder than the underlying metal, so wear accelerates as the harder particles abrade the metal surfaces further. Fretting corrosion acts in the same way, especially when water is present. Unprotected bearings on large structures like bridges can suffer serious degradation in behaviour, especially when salt is used the during winter to deice the highways carried by the bridges. The problem of fretting corrosion was involved in the Silver Bridge tragedy and the Mianus River Bridge accident.

paper_did: Deposited CoCrFeNiMo high‐entropy alloy coatings on Q355 steel substrates using coaxial powder‐fed laser cladding.
Systematically varied laser power (1750, 2000, 2250, and 2500 W) while keeping other parameters constant to investigate its effect on microstructure, defect formation, and interfacial bonding.
Characterized the coatings comprehensively via XRD, optical microscopy, SEM/EDS, microhardness mapping, wear testing (reciprocating sliding), and corrosion testing (potentiodynamic polarization).
paper_reported: Identified that the coatings develop a dual‐phase microstructure consisting of an FCC matrix and dispersed Mo‐rich σ phases, with the optimum coating quality (minimal defects, low porosity, strong metallurgical bonding) observed at 2250 W.

Found that laser power critically affects dilution with the substrate (increase in Fe incorporation), grain morphology (evolution from coarse to refined and lamellar structures) and the overall balance between hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion behavior.

Reported that the friction mechanism involves in-situ formation then rupture of a protective oxide film (leading to adhesive and abrasive wear), while the corrosion mechanism is governed by galvanic coupling between the FCC phase and the σ phase.
paper_proposed: Highlighted the need for systematic studies with univariate regulation (e.g. laser power gradient studies) to better elucidate the process–structure–property relationships.

Suggested exploring processing routes that balance enhanced hardness (via σ-phase precipitation) with minimized galvanic corrosion and defect formation, potentially through optimizing processing parameters or post-deposition treatments.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The accelerated coupled degradation arises from a wear-induced breakdown of a transient protective oxide film on the multi-phase eutectic HEA, where the inherent galvanic coupling between the hard, Mo-rich σ phase and the softer, FCC matrix intensifies local anodic dissolution. Repeated mechanical removal of the oxide exposes fresh interfaces with potential differences, which in turn accelerate corrosion and further impair the wear resistance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix and dispersed Mo-rich σ phases that naturally form galvanic microcells.
hypotheses.intervention: Prepare two alloy variants: one with the standard microstructural heterogeneity and another with a modified heat treatment designed to reduce the potential difference between the σ and FCC phases (e.g., by promoting homogenization of element distribution).
hypotheses.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., > 600 °C) environment under simultaneous wear (reciprocating sliding) and corrosive exposure (chloride-containing electrolyte or controlled oxidizing atmosphere).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The interphase boundaries between the σ phase and FCC matrix that act as galvanic couples and the integrity of the protective oxide film.
hypotheses.mechanism: Under high-temperature tribocorrosion, mechanical wear repeatedly ruptures the initially forming protective oxide layer. This exposes the underlying phases with distinct electrochemical potentials. The σ phase (being more noble due to Mo enrichment) and the FCC phase form galvanic cells, accelerating anodic dissolution in the FCC regions. The local corrosion further undermines the oxide reformation, infecting the wear interface with pitting and accelerating overall material loss. The cycle of oxide removal, local galvanic corrosion and wear leads to a synergistically increased degradation rate.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the homogenized variant, the standard heterogeneous microstructure will exhibit a significantly higher total degradation, with markedly increased wear volume (potentially on the order of several times that of the baseline) and elevated corrosion current density. The modified alloy with reduced potential differences should show a lower wear-corrosion synergy.
hypotheses.baseline: The untreated multi-phase eutectic HEA with its natural galvanic potential difference and corresponding coupled wear-corrosion degradation.
hypotheses.boundary: Elevated operating temperatures, where a protective oxide film would typically form, and environments that facilitate both mechanical abrasion and corrosive attack.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact amplification factor of the degradation rates is uncertain due to possible variations in oxide film kinetics and local potential differences; however, the trend of increased degradation for the heterogeneous case is expected.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct accelerated wear–corrosion tests at elevated temperatures on two sets of samples: one with the standard HEA microstructure and one with a post-heat-treatment homogenized microstructure designed to minimize phase potential differences. Monitor both the wear volume and the corrosion current (using electrochemical measurements) over time.
measurements: Wear volume via white-light interferometry
Corrosion current density via potentiodynamic polarization
Surface oxide integrity via SEM/EDS mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized alloy (with reduced interphase potential differences) does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in coupled degradation—i.e., similar wear and corrosion rates as the standard alloy—the hypothesis that galvanic coupling from oxide film breakdown is the primary accelerator is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The finding in the paper that the σ phase enhances hardness but also induces galvanic corrosion effects (PMC12156342::web::006::1_introduction; PMC12156342::web::007::1_introduction) and the known protective role of oxide films in high-temperature corrosion (TXT::wikipedia::High-temperature_corrosion::014).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis explicitly links the mechanical removal of an evolving oxide film with enhanced galvanic coupling between phases, proposing a control through microstructural homogenization—a route not explored in the paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The coupled degradation is accelerated by wear-enhanced local compositional changes that trigger detrimental phase transformations at the contact surface, where mechanical abrasion promotes preferential removal of surface-enriched elements and triggers further precipitation of the brittle σ phase, thereby compromising both corrosion resistance and wear integrity.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase microstructure consisting of an FCC matrix and dispersed Mo-rich σ phases.
hypotheses.intervention: Implement a controlled cooling rate variation during processing to purposely produce a gradient in σ phase distribution at the surface versus the bulk. Compare samples with a surface layer enriched in σ phase (via rapid cooling) to samples with a more uniform phase distribution achieved by optimized cooling.
hypotheses.conditions: Simultaneous exposure to elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–700 °C), mechanical wear (using reciprocating sliding tests), and a corrosive medium (e.g., NaCl solution or oxidizing gas), where surface composition can evolve due to wear.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The surface phase distribution and the local concentration of Mo and Fe, which control the precipitation of additional brittle σ phase and the formation of less protective corrosion products.
hypotheses.mechanism: Mechanical wear preferentially removes the more ductile FCC phase from the contact zone, leaving behind a surface enriched in σ phase. This altered composition further promotes the formation and growth of additional brittle σ precipitates during high-temperature operation. The increased σ phase fraction, while initially beneficial for hardness, leads to a more inhomogeneous and brittle surface that becomes more susceptible to crack initiation under stress and has poorer corrosion resistance due to suboptimal passivation. This results in an accelerated overall degradation that is a synergistic consequence of both increased wear (owing to brittle microcrack propagation) and enhanced corrosion from an unstable surface chemistry.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The σ phase–enriched surface is expected to show a modest reduction in overall wear resistance (with increased microcracking and material spalling) and a noticeable increase in corrosion current density, leading to an overall degradation rate that is significantly higher (potentially 1.5–2×) compared to a uniform phase distribution baseline.
hypotheses.baseline: Samples produced with an optimized cooling rate that yields a homogeneous dual-phase structure throughout the material thickness, minimizing surface compositional gradients.
hypotheses.boundary: High temperature and corrosive environments where wear-induced compositional changes are significant; limited to processing conditions that allow for controlled cooling rate interventions.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the trend is supported by phase transformation principles, the quantitative effect of surface σ phase enrichment on the degradation rates remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with different cooling rates: one inducing a surface σ phase enrichment and one yielding a uniform phase distribution. Subject both sets to identical wear-corrosion tests at elevated temperatures, and measure the wear-induced phase composition change using surface analysis techniques (e.g., XRD, SEM/EDS) alongside corrosion testing.
measurements: Surface phase composition via XRD and SEM/EDS
Wear volume and crack density via white-light interferometry/SEM
Corrosion current density via electrochemical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with surface σ phase enrichment do not exhibit a statistically higher degradation rate and a degraded corrosion response compared to the uniform samples, the hypothesis that wear-enhanced compositional changes lead to detrimental phase transformations driving accelerated degradation is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation that the σ phase enhances hardness while also contributing to galvanic corrosion (PMC12156342::web::006::1_introduction; PMC12156342::web::014::3_1_phase_composition_and_microstructure) combined with the background on eutectic phase spacing affecting mechanical performance (TXT::wikipedia::Eutectic_system::008).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the concept that wear itself can induce a local compositional and phase transformation at the surface, thereby driving a feedback loop that exacerbates degradation—an idea not treated in the paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation is driven by thermomechanical fatigue arising from cyclic thermal expansion mismatch between the FCC and σ phases under elevated temperature, which is further amplified by wear; the cyclic stress causes microcracking and spallation at phase boundaries, thereby exposing fresh surfaces to aggressive corrosion, and the resulting pits act as stress concentrators that enhance wear.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy with inherently different coefficients of thermal expansion between the FCC matrix and the harder σ phase.
hypotheses.intervention: Design a controlled study that adjusts the residual thermal stresses via a post-deposition heat treatment (e.g., a subcritical anneal) aimed at reducing the thermal mismatch between phases. Compare the mechanically polished as-clad HEA with the post-treated HEA.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposure to high temperatures (e.g., 600–700 °C) and cyclic thermal loading combined with continuous sliding wear in a corrosive environment, conditions under which differential thermal expansion becomes significant.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The phase boundaries between the FCC and σ phases and the residual interlayer stresses built during rapid processing.
hypotheses.mechanism: Under cyclic heating (or sustained elevated temperature coupled with mechanical frictional heating), the mismatch in thermal expansion between the FCC and σ phases generates cyclic stresses at their interfaces. These stresses initiate microcracks along the phase boundaries. The concurrent wear process then exacerbates these microcracks by mechanically removing loosely attached fragments. The microcracks expose fresh metal to the corrosive environment, leading to accelerated corrosion (especially galvanic in nature given the phase differences). The cumulative effect of microcracking, wear-induced spallation, and accelerated localized corrosion results in coupled degradation that is significantly more rapid than the sum of the individual effects.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The as-clad alloys with higher residual thermal stresses and pronounced thermal expansion mismatch will show a higher degradation rate, with increased microcrack density, spallation, and higher corrosion currents compared to the post-heat-treated, stress-relieved samples. Total degradation is predicted to increase notably (potentially >2×) in the high-stress samples.
hypotheses.baseline: The untreated, as-clad HEA with its inherent residual stresses and thermal expansion mismatch between phases.
hypotheses.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions of elevated temperature and cyclic thermal/mechanical loading where differential thermal expansion is pronounced; not applicable at room temperature or under static conditions.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative measures of the degradation amplification due to thermal expansion mismatches are difficult to precisely predict; the directional trend (increased degradation with higher stress) is robust but the exact factor is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one as-clad (with high residual thermal stresses) and one subjected to a subcritical annealing to relieve thermal stresses. Subject both to cyclic elevated temperature wear–corrosion tests and use non-destructive evaluation (e.g., acoustic emission, micro-CT) to monitor microcrack development along with standard wear and corrosion measurements.
measurements: Residual stress measurement via X-ray diffraction
Microcrack density using acoustic emission or micro-CT
Wear volume and corrosion current density measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the stress-relieved samples do not display a statistically lower microcrack density, wear rate, and corrosion rate compared to the as-clad samples under the same test conditions, the hypothesis that cyclic thermal expansion mismatch is driving the accelerated degradation is falsified.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces cyclic thermal expansion mismatch as a key driver of microcracking and coupled degradation in a multi-phase HEA under wear – a mechanism distinct from purely galvanic or compositional change effects discussed in the paper.

sound.reason: The hypothesis directly builds on the paper’s findings that an oxide film forms and ruptures during wear and that galvanic coupling between the FCC and σ phases accelerates corrosion, making the mechanism consistent with established principles.

testable.reason: The proposed experiment—with two alloy variants (a standard heterogeneous microstructure and one modified by heat treatment for homogenization) evaluated under elevated temperature wear–corrosion conditions using wear volume, corrosion current density, and surface oxide analyses—is clear and controllable.

beyond_paper.reason: It extends the paper’s static characterization by proposing a dynamic, cyclic mechanism where repeated removal of the protective oxide leads to renewed galvanic corrosion, and it introduces a route (microstructural homogenization) to mitigate this effect that was not explored in the study.

paper_did: Prepared an industrial‐scale (~2.5 kg) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy by conventional casting using commercially pure elements.
Achieved a uniform, fine lamellar dual‐phase microstructure consisting of soft fcc and hard B2 phases with an interlamellar spacing of about 2 μm.
Characterized the alloy’s microstructure (using SEM/EDS, XRD, DSC) and measured its density.
Conducted mechanical tests including room‐temperature and high‐temperature (600–700°C) tensile tests, plus thermomechanical modification via cold rolling.
paper_reported: An unprecedented combination of high fracture strength (true fracture stress ~1.2 GPa) and high ductility (elongation ~23–25%) at room temperature.
Maintenance of excellent mechanical properties and ultrahigh strain hardening even at elevated temperatures up to 700°C.
The fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure that enables efficient dislocation storage and interface pinning, leading to significant work hardening.
Superior castability, low compositional segregation, and a lower overall density compared to traditional Ni‐based high‐temperature alloys.
paper_proposed: Future exploration of new EHEA compositions based on physical metallurgy principles using parameters such as atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration.
Employing thermodynamic methods (e.g., CALPHAD) and pseudo‐binary alloy system assumptions to pinpoint eutectic compositions.
Further tuning of mechanical properties through controlled processing routes and thermomechanical treatments.

Characterized the microstructure and phase evolution by XRD, SEM, and TEM—showing a single-phase FCC solid solution for low copper (0–5 at.%) and the precipitation of a copper‐rich secondary FCC2 phase for higher copper (10–20 at.%).

Performed tribological (pin-on-disk tests measuring wear volume, friction, hardness, elastic modulus) and corrosion (polarization tests in 3.5% NaCl) experiments to correlate mechanical properties, wear behavior, and corrosion resistance with copper-induced phase segregation.
paper_reported: Reported that the solubility limit of copper in the CoCrFeNi matrix is approximately 9 at.%—with complete dissolution at 5 at.% and phase segregation (forming a soft, copper‐rich FCC2 phase) at Cu ≥10 at.%.

Found that a moderate copper addition (5 at.%) improves wear resistance (23% reduction in wear volume) via solid solution hardening, while excess copper leads to decreased hardness and increased wear due to the formation of a soft secondary phase.

Showed that corrosion behavior is sensitive to copper content: lower Cu (with fully dissolved Cu) leads to lower corrosion resistance (attributed to formation of detrimental Cu₂O), whereas higher Cu (with a duplex FCC1 + FCC2 structure) mitigates galvanic corrosion by coarsening the FCC2 phase and reducing interfacial contact area.
paper_proposed: The paper does not explicitly propose follow‐up experiments or future work; it primarily establishes the role of copper content and phase morphology on wear and corrosion properties.

paper_did: Synthesized an equiatomic CrMoNbWV high‐entropy alloy (HEA) from elemental powders via mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at three different temperatures (1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C).

Characterized the alloy’s microstructure using XRD and SEM/EDS, showing a primary BCC solid solution with partial decomposition into Laves phases (Cr2Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb) and oxide phases (NbVO4–VO), with evident grain coarsening and carburization effects from the graphite die during SPS.
Tested mechanical properties (compressive strength, hardness), wear behavior (using ASTM G65 abrasion tests) and corrosion resistance (electrochemical tests in 0.5 M H2SO4 at room temperature).
paper_reported: The MA powders yielded a BCC structure that, after SPS, partially decomposed into Laves phases and oxide precipitates; the volume fraction of the brittle Laves phases decreased with increasing sintering temperature while oxide morphology changed (with coarser oxides at higher temperature).

The sintered HEA exhibited high compressive strength (2700–2870 MPa) and good wear and corrosion resistance, although low plasticity was observed due to the intergranular localization of brittle phases.
Carburization during SPS (via carbon diffusion from the graphite die) resulted in interstitial carbon incorporation and carbide formation in the surface layer, which modified local wear properties.
paper_proposed: Future work will focus on using iron‐free powders, investigating the effect of SPS duration, and applying additional post‐process heat treatments to further refine the alloy’s structure and properties.

paper_did: Manufactured a refractory CrMoNbWV high‐entropy alloy (HEA) using mechanical alloying of elemental powders (Nb, Mo, W, V, Cr in equiatomic ratios) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C.

Performed microstructural characterization (XRD, SEM, EDS) to identify a BCC solid solution in the MA‐powder and its partial decomposition during SPS into Laves phases (Cr2Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb) and NbVO4–VO oxide precipitates; observed grain coarsening and carburization effects with increasing sintering temperature.

Conducted mechanical testing (compressive strength, microhardness), wear tests (according to ASTM G65), and electrochemical corrosion tests in 0.5 M H2SO4 to evaluate the alloy’s strength, wear resistance, and corrosion behavior.
paper_reported: The as‐synthesized HEA exhibited a predominantly BCC solid solution with secondary phases; sintering at higher temperatures reduced the volume fraction of Laves phases and changed oxide morphology, affecting grain size and hardness.
The alloy showed high compressive strength (2700–2870 MPa) and commendable wear and corrosion resistance, with differences noted between the carburized surface layer and the bulk material.

Mechanistic insights were provided on how the presence and distribution of Laves phases and oxides (particularly at grain boundaries) influence brittleness and degradation, with a discussion on the impact of processing temperature on phase evolution.
paper_proposed: Future work will focus on eliminating iron contamination in the starting powder, studying the effect of SPS dwell time (i.e. the duration effect of the SPS process), and investigating additional post‐process heat treatments to further modify the microstructure and optimize the alloy’s properties.

paper_did: Synthesized an equiatomic CrMoNbWV high‐entropy alloy (HEA) from elemental powders (Nb, Mo, W, V, and Cr) using mechanical alloying (5 h) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C under 50 MPa for 5 min.

Characterized the microstructure via X‐ray diffraction, SEM, and chemical analysis to reveal a BCC solid solution that partially decomposed during SPS into Laves phases (Cr2Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb) and oxide precipitates (NbVO4–VO).

Assessed mechanical properties (compressive strength ~2700–2870 MPa, hardness), wear performance (using ASTM G65 test conditions), and corrosion behavior (electrochemical tests in 0.5 M H2SO4) of the produced samples.

Identified that increasing the sintering temperature leads to grain coarsening, a reduction in the volume fraction of Laves phases, changes in oxide morphology, and the formation of a carburized surface layer (due to carbon diffusion from the graphite die).
paper_reported: The MA‐derived CrMoNbWV HEA primarily forms a BCC solid solution that partly decomposes during SPS into brittle Laves phases and oxides, with the phase fractions and grain morphology dependent on sintering temperature.
High mechanical performance with compressive strengths of ~2700–2870 MPa was achieved, although low plasticity results from the brittle intergranular phases.

Wear tests showed that the carburized layer (formed due to carbon uptake) exhibits superior wear resistance compared to the bulk alloy, and corrosion tests in 0.5 M H2SO4 indicate good passivation behavior.

The observed microstructural evolution (e.g., reduction of Laves phase content with higher SPS temperature and coarsening of oxide inclusions) is linked to the corresponding changes in mechanical and corrosion properties.
paper_proposed: Obtain a powder with reduced iron contamination.
Investigate the effect of varying SPS duration on the HEA’s microstructure and properties.
Examine additional post‐processing heat treatments to further manipulate phase distribution and optimize material performance.

paper_did: Fabricated cladding coatings on SS-304 by depositing an equiatomic blend (20 wt% each of Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu) prepared via ball-milling and applied using a microwave hybrid heating process (900 W, 2.45 GHz) with a charcoal susceptor.
Exposed the coated samples to thermal treatment in air at 800 °C for up to 10 weeks and performed detailed microstructural examinations using SEM and optical microscopy.

Conducted mechanical and chemical testing – including Vickers hardness measurements, XRD phase analysis, corrosion immersion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl (ASTM G44), and pin-on-disc wear tests under specified loading and sliding conditions.
paper_reported: The formation of a uniform cladding layer with enhanced surface hardness and wear resistance, attributed to the emergence of harder phases (e.g., FeNi3, Al2O3, etc.).

The evolution of protective surface layers during thermal exposure, in particular the formation of a Cr2O3 barrier and a high-entropy spinel ((Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4) coating, which contribute to improved thermostability and corrosion resistance.
The occurrence of micro-fractures or cracks (notably at the cladding/substrate interface) likely due to differential cooling rates and residual stresses from the microwave cladding process.
paper_proposed: Future investigations focused on optimizing various microwave cladding parameters – such as substrate pre-heating, metallic powder content, irradiation duration, and environmental conditions – to further enhance coating quality.

paper_did: Fabricated two complex concentrated alloys (Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 referred to as NiX and Ni75(AlNbTiV)25 referred to as Ni3X) via mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS).

Characterized the microstructure in detail using BF‐TEM, HRTEM, HAADF-STEM, SAED, and EDS to reveal nano-coupled grains, hierarchical nanoprecipitates, phase distributions, and composition undulations.

Conducted sliding wear tests under a wide temperature range (from room temperature up to 800 °C) under constant load, and performed complementary measurements (Vickers hardness, nanoindentation with H/E and H³/E² analyses) to correlate tribological performance with microstructural evolution.

Examined the wear-induced microstructural evolution, including the formation of a gradient, recrystallized tribo-layer at room temperature and the generation of a dense, protective glaze (oxide) layer at elevated temperatures.
paper_reported: NiX (the high-alloying concentration variant) exhibited ultra-low wear rates (on the order of 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁶ mm³/Nm) over the entire tested temperature range, while Ni3X suffered higher wear due to conventional abrasive and adhesive mechanisms.

The exceptional wear resistance of NiX is attributed to its unique nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation, which enables adaptive friction interface protection through stage-wise stress relief via gradient recrystallization at room temperature and continuous formation of a dense glaze layer at high temperature.

Detailed analyses (e.g., SEM observations of worn tracks and nanoindentation of inside/outside worn regions) confirm that the integrity and stability of the glaze layer are key to minimizing adhesive and oxidative wear at high temperatures.
paper_proposed: Future work should aim to clarify the origin and formation mechanism of the nanohierarchical architecture, particularly the multicomponent solutal response during the MA and SPS processes, through additional simulations and experiments.

Further investigations are suggested to optimize the interplay between intrinsic composition undulations and tribo-chemical reactions to tailor friction interface protection over a wide temperature range.

paper_did: Fabricated ferritic stainless steel (FSS 430) specimens using laser powder directed energy deposition (LP-DED), varying laser powers (500, 600, and 700 W) and hatch distances (0.8, 1.2, and 1.4 mm).
Applied two distinct solution heat treatment regimes (815 °C and 980 °C for 1 hour followed by forced fan cooling) to both LP-DED deposits and a commercial AISI 430 plate.
Performed comprehensive characterization including microstructural analysis (SEM, EBSD), Rockwell hardness testing, and dry sliding wear tests at 25 °C and 300 °C using a ball-on-flat configuration.
paper_reported: Observed that solution heat treatment at 980 °C induces full recrystallization with enhanced carbide (chrome-rich) precipitation along grain boundaries, resulting in increased hardness.

Found a strong correlation between increased hardness (influenced by laser energy input and heat treatment) and improved wear resistance, as evidenced by lower friction coefficients, reduced wear depth, and smaller wear areas.

Determined that higher laser power and optimized hatch spacing yield better inter-track bonding and microstructural homogeneity, which in turn mitigates abrasive and adhesive wear phenomena (including aspects of tribo-oxidation) under the test conditions.
paper_proposed: Investigating the high‐temperature wear properties pertinent to labyrinth seal applications, potentially operating around 500 °C.
Further optimizing LP‐DED processing parameters and post‐processing heat treatments to tailor the microstructure and enhance wear resistance under simultaneous mechanical and thermal loading.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation in the multi‐phase eutectic HEA arises because incoherent phase boundaries promote the formation of fragile, non-adherent oxide scales that are prone to spallation under cyclic wear. The repeatedly spalled oxide exposes fresh, vulnerable metal surfaces, which then oxidize rapidly and further aggravate wear.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with inherently heterogeneous microstructure including distinct phases with incoherent interfaces.
hypotheses.intervention: Implement a post-solidification heat treatment designed to promote coarsening and partial coalescence of carbide or intermetallic precipitates to achieve more coherent phase boundaries.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosive environments at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 500 °C) where oxide formation and spallation are relevant.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Improved coherence and bonding at phase boundaries leading to better oxide adhesion and reduced localized interfacial stress.
hypotheses.mechanism: In the baseline alloy, heterogeneous interfaces accelerate damage by forming fragile oxide scales that crack and spall under mechanical loading. The heat treatment reduces interface mismatch, minimizing spallation. Reduced spallation limits fresh metal exposure and hence lowers both the wear and corrosion rates.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline, the treated alloy should exhibit lower total degradation with reduced wear volume and lower corrosion rates (directionally improved wear and corrosion resistance, with an anticipated improvement in degradation metrics on the order of a moderate percentage, although exact values are uncertain).
hypotheses.baseline: As-deposited multi-phase eutectic HEA with incoherent phase boundaries yielding fragile oxide scales and accelerated spallation.
hypotheses.boundary: Tested under elevated temperatures (~500 °C) in a corrosive (oxygen-containing) atmosphere combined with cyclic mechanical wear.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement is predicted qualitatively; precise numerical changes require experimental calibration.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation is driven by differential phase wear in the eutectic HEA: A softer phase preferentially wears away, leaving harder phases protruding and setting up localized galvanic couples. The resulting potential differences at phase interfaces exacerbate both localized corrosion and mechanical removal.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic HEA with phases exhibiting different hardness and electrical potentials, leading to an intrinsic micro-galvanic system.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce minor microalloying additions (e.g., boron) to homogenize the hardness and alter the electrochemical behavior at phase boundaries, thereby reducing galvanic potential differences.
hypotheses.conditions: Simultaneous exposure to wear and corrosive environments at elevated temperature (e.g., 500 °C), where differences in phase hardness and stability are pronounced.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: More uniform distribution of hardness and reduced potential gradients at phase boundaries due to altered grain boundary chemistry.
hypotheses.mechanism: In the untreated alloy, uneven wear causes softer phase removal and exposes harder, nobler phases that become anodic relative to their surroundings. This galvanic mismatch accelerates corrosion locally, and the resulting degradation further enhances wear. The boron addition is expected to refine and equalize microstructural hardness, reducing galvanic coupling and hence the synergy between wear and corrosion.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the boron-modified alloy should exhibit a lower overall degradation rate with decreased wear volume and mitigated corrosion at the phase interfaces (direction: improvement; precise reduction magnitude remains uncertain).
hypotheses.baseline: Eutectic HEA without boron addition, where constituent phases differ significantly in mechanical and electrochemical properties.
hypotheses.boundary: Samples evaluated under the same elevated temperature (≈500 °C) and corrosive-cum-wear conditions with controlled sliding contact.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the directional improvements are supported by analogous behavior in Ni3Al alloys, the precise quantitative difference is uncertain.

paper_did: Synthesized AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy via arc melting, suction-casting, and subsequent thermo‐mechanical processing.
Employed a novel hybrid‐rolling process combining cryo‐rolling (ε ≈ 1.2) and warm‐rolling at 600 °C (ε ≈ 1.2) to achieve a total strain of ~2.4 (90% thickness reduction).

Characterized the microstructure using EBSD, TEM, HAADF-STEM, and nano-beam diffraction, revealing retained lamellar regions (ordered L12 and B2 phases) alongside transformed nanocrystalline regions with compositional variations.
Performed tensile tests that established an outstanding mechanical performance with yield strength (σYS ~1900 MPa), ultimate tensile strength (σUTS ~2000 MPa), and uniform elongation (~8%).
paper_reported: The hybrid-rolled alloy exhibits an unprecedented combination of high strength and acceptable ductility in bulk form.

A dual structural-compositional heterogeneous microstructure is formed, wherein retained lamellar regions and adjacent nanocrystalline regions contain distinct ordered/disordered phases with varying chemical compositions.

The outstanding mechanical properties are primarily attributed to mechanisms such as nanostructuring and the generation of long-range back stress from the high density of interfaces and strain gradients.
paper_proposed: Future work will focus on quantifying the back stress and further tuning the microstructural heterogeneities to enhance the mechanical performance.
The novel hybrid processing route is proposed for exploitation in tailoring the nanostructure and properties of other multiphase/dual-phase high entropy alloys.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Galvanic couples formed at heterogeneous phase boundaries accelerate wear–corrosion degradation under elevated temperature by enhancing local electrochemical activity when protective oxides are mechanically removed.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: Abundant heterointerfaces between dissimilar phases with distinct electrochemical potentials.
hypotheses.mechanism: Differing electrochemical potentials between the phases cause local galvanic cells. During wear, the mechanical removal of protective oxides at these interfaces repeatedly exposes fresh metal, thereby intensifying local anodic dissolution. Elevated temperature further speeds up diffusion and reaction rates, leading to an accelerated coupled degradation process.

hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in degradation and the sensitivity to minor differences in interfacial area are not fully determined.

paper_did: Synthesized an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy via arc melting and suction casting.
Processed the alloy using a novel hybrid‐rolling route consisting of sequential cryo‐rolling (ε ~1.2) and warm‐rolling at 600 °C (ε ~1.2) to achieve a total strain of ~2.4 (90% thickness reduction).

Characterized the microstructure extensively using SEM, EBSD, TEM, STEM, and EDS, revealing dual structural–compositional heterogeneities with lamellar regions (ordered L12 and B2 phases) coexisting with nanocrystalline regions.
Measured mechanical properties including yield strength (~1900 MPa), ultimate tensile strength (~2000 MPa) and uniform elongation (~8%), demonstrating an unprecedented strength–ductility synergy.
paper_reported: The hybrid‐rolled EHEA has an exceptional combination of high strength (σYS ~1900 MPa, σUTS ~2000 MPa) and appreciable ductility (~8%), outperforming both the as‐cast and cryo‐rolled states.

The dual structural–compositional heterogeneous microstructure (lamellar regions with ordered L12 and B2 and nanocrystalline regions with varied compositions) is responsible for the enhanced mechanical properties, primarily via back-stress strengthening and multiple deformation mechanisms.

It was observed that during processing, stored energy from the cryo-rolling accelerates microstructural transformations during subsequent warm-rolling, leading to the observed phase and compositional variations.
paper_proposed: Future work will involve quantifying the back-stress and its role in the mechanical performance of the hybrid-rolled EHEA.
The authors envisage further exploiting the hybrid processing strategy to tune the nanostructure and properties of a wide range of dual- and multiphase high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Differential Oxide Film Formation and Spallation Drives Accelerated Degradation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring dual structural‐compositional heterogeneities; coarse, well-ordered lamellar regions (ordered L12 and B2) coexist with nanocrystalline regions with higher diffusivity and variable composition.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment at an intermediate temperature that forms a uniform, adherent oxide layer on both regions without significantly altering the bulk microstructure.
hypotheses.conditions: Simultaneous wear and corrosive exposure at elevated temperature where transient oxide films are normally disrupted mechanically.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The interface between lamellar and nanocrystalline regions where oxide films differ in thickness, adhesion, and composition.
hypotheses.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the rapid diffusion in nanocrystalline zones leads to fast but nonuniform oxide formation that produces a thicker, poorly adherent oxide than the lamellar regions, where slower oxidation yields a thinner, more protective film. During wear, the mechanical removal of these disparate oxides results in repeated breakdown and repair cycles. The mismatch in oxide quality at interfaces causes stress concentration and spallation of the oxide film, thereby exposing fresh metal surfaces to accelerated corrosive attack. This alternation between wear-induced oxide removal and rapid, nonprotective re-oxidation is hypothesized to couple wear and corrosion, enhancing overall degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy that forms heterogeneous oxides naturally, the pre-oxidized sample should exhibit a more uniform and adherent oxide film, leading to lower corrosion pit densities and reduced overall degradation (with similar wear rates but a measurable decrease in corrosion-driven mass loss).
hypotheses.baseline: The as-processed dual heterogeneous alloy, in which oxide formation is dictated by the intrinsic differences in diffusion kinetics between lamellar and nanocrystalline regions.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate when the operating temperature is high enough to induce rapid oxidation (yet below temperatures causing bulk microstructural changes) and when mechanical wear repeatedly disrupts the naturally forming, mismatched oxide films.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise differences in oxide film properties between the phases and the quantitative improvement achievable with pre-oxidation treatment remain to be established.

paper_did: Fabricated AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (with x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding with high-purity gas‐atomized elemental powders.
Varied the boron content to induce in situ formation of TiB2 and to modify the microstructure (dendritic and interdendritic regions) without altering the primary BCC and σ phases.
Characterized the coatings using XRD, SEM, and EDS to determine phase composition, morphology, and elemental distribution.

Measured microhardness, performed room‐temperature wear tests (analyzing friction coefficients, wear rates, and worn surface morphology), and assessed corrosion resistance via electrochemical tests (potentiodynamic polarization and EIS) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.
paper_reported: B addition preserves the base BCC and σ phases while promoting the formation of in situ TiB2, which refines the BCC phase and alters the phase size and morphology with increasing B content.

Microhardness increases with B content and the optimum wear resistance is achieved at x = 1; however, excessive boron (x = 1.5) leads to agglomerated TiB2 particles that spall under wear, undermining performance.

Corrosion resistance improves with a small amount of boron (x = 0.5) due to a more stable passive film, but excessive boron degrades film integrity due to the defects introduced by large TiB2 clusters.
The study links microstructural features (e.g., grain refinement, TiB2 particle distribution) to performance improvements and provides a basis for further optimization.
paper_proposed: Further optimization of the coating’s performance through compositional tuning and post‐processing to address specific service environments, machinability, and long‐term stability.
Expansion of the generalized design strategy for high-performance HEA coatings to enable reliable service across a broad range of applications.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Phase Boundary Oxide Disruption Accelerates Degradation due to Selective Passive Film Breakdown at Heterogeneous Interfaces.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting heterogeneous phase distribution with inherent phase boundaries that form distinct passive films under ambient conditions.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the alloy chemistry by minor reactive microalloying (e.g., trace boron addition) that preferentially segregates at phase boundaries to improve the adhesion and stability of the passive oxide film.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (e.g., above 300°C) where oxidation kinetics are enhanced and mechanical abrasion is significant.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The chemical composition and integrity of the passive oxide film at phase boundaries between the eutectic phases.
hypotheses.mechanism: At elevated temperature, wear mechanically removes sections of the incipient passive oxide film. The heterogeneous chemical and structural nature of the eutectic phases causes the passive film to form unevenly. Without stabilization, once removed, the exposed phase boundaries undergo rapid oxidation and localized corrosion. Boron segregation can tie together the interface, promoting a more continuous and adherent passive layer, thereby reducing film breakdown and subsequent galvanic corrosion. This interplay of micro-scale film disruption and local galvanic effects leads to accelerated overall degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy without boron, the boron-doped alloy should exhibit a lower total degradation rate. Individually, the wear rate and corrosion current density should decrease due to improved passive film stability at the vulnerable phase boundaries. Expected improvements are moderate (~20–30% reduction in degradation metrics), though precise values are uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Multi-phase eutectic HEA without microalloying additives, showing localized film breakdown at phase boundaries under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: Effective only during high-temperature operation (above ambient, e.g., >300°C) and under simultaneous mechanical wear conditions; the beneficial effect of boron may vanish under low-temperature or static conditions.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact degree of improvement in passive film stability and the quantitative reduction in degradation rates remain to be determined experimentally.

Characterize passive film integrity via surface microscopy and measure degradation rates via wear tracks and electrochemical tests.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Coarse Eutectic Spacing Amplifies Degradation via Enhanced Interface Exposure and Localized Oxidation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with relatively coarse interlamellar or discontinuous eutectic structures, featuring large phase boundaries that serve as sites for passive film formation.
hypotheses.intervention: Process modification to refine the eutectic spacing—achieved by increasing the cooling rate during solidification or by adding microalloying elements (other than boron) known to promote nucleation—thereby reducing the size of the individual eutectic colonies.
hypotheses.conditions: Operational conditions combine elevated temperature (to speed up oxidation kinetics) with mechanical wear in corrosive environments.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The size and distribution of the eutectic phases and their interphase boundaries that control the area and continuity of the passive oxide film.
hypotheses.mechanism: Coarse eutectic spacing results in extensive, contiguous phase boundaries where passive oxide films are formed. Under wear, these large interfacial areas are more susceptible to mechanical rupture and localized removal of the film, leading to accelerated corrosion at the interfaces. Refining the eutectic spacing reduces the effective phase boundary area susceptible to film breakdown. A more homogenous and fine-scale microstructure distributes stresses more evenly during wear, thereby diminishing localized damage and slowing corrosion initiation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy with coarse eutectic structures, the refined microstructure should show a reduction in both overall degradation and in separate wear and corrosion metrics. The anticipated outcome is a moderated decrease in total degradation (e.g., wear rate and corrosion current density) though the precise magnitude is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: The same multi-phase eutectic HEA produced via conventional cooling rates leading to coarse eutectic spacing, which exhibits accelerated degradation due to extensive interface exposure.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant under conditions where the cooling rate during processing can be reliably controlled and where the operating temperature is high enough to activate oxidation processes.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative reductions in degradation rates are subject to experimental verification and may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing limits.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Thermally Induced Residual Stress Cracking at Phase Interfaces Drives Accelerated Degradation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy containing phases with mismatched thermal expansion coefficients, generating inherent residual stresses at phase interfaces during processing.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: The density and distribution of microcracks at phase interfaces induced by thermal expansion mismatch and exacerbated by mechanical wear.
hypotheses.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the different phases within the eutectic HEA expand at different rates due to mismatched thermal expansion coefficients. The resulting residual stresses concentrate at the interfaces leading to the formation of microcracks. These microcracks serve as preferential sites for both mechanical wear penetration and accelerated corrosion due to increased exposure of fresh, unoxidized material. This coupled mechanism of residual stress-induced cracking and subsequent degradation accelerates overall material loss.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: When compared to a baseline alloy with higher mismatch (and thus higher crack density), the modified alloy with reduced thermal expansion mismatch should display fewer interfacial cracks, resulting in lower wear rates and lower corrosion current densities. The overall degradation should be measurably reduced, though the exact percentage reduction is uncertain.

hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is most relevant under conditions involving significant thermal cycling and high service temperatures; its impact may be diminished in isothermal conditions.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the formation of residual stresses and microcracks is well-understood, the quantification of their contribution to overall degradation in these alloys under service conditions remains to be precisely determined.

paper_did: Fabricated AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx high‐entropy alloy coatings on Q235 steel substrates via laser cladding with varied boron additions (x = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5).

Characterized the coatings’ microstructure using XRD, SEM, and EDS to reveal the retention of BCC and σ phases, the in situ formation of TiB2 particles, and the dendritic–interdendritic (DR–IR) segregation.

Conducted mechanical and electrochemical tests—including microhardness measurements, wear tests (friction coefficient, wear rate, and wear morphology) and corrosion evaluations (potentiodynamic polarization and EIS in 3.5 wt.% NaCl)—to correlate microstructural features with wear and corrosion resistance.
paper_reported: Boron addition induces the in situ formation of TiB2 particles whose size and volume fraction increase with B content, leading to significant lattice distortion and refinement of the BCC phase.

Enhanced microhardness and improved wear resistance (best performance at x = 1) were achieved via a combination of fine TiB2 dispersion, solid solution, and grain refinement effects, while excessive B (e.g., x = 1.5) promoted TiB2 agglomeration that spalls and degrades performance.

Corrosion tests showed that trace B additions improve passive film stability and reduce corrosion current density (icorr), whereas excessive B leads to passive film defects that accelerate pitting and galvanic corrosion.
paper_proposed: Future work is suggested to further optimize the coating through compositional tuning and post‐processing, and to explore performance aspects such as long‐term stability, machinability, and behavior under specific service environments.

hypotheses.hypothesis: TiB2 Agglomeration‐Induced Passive Film Disruption Accelerates Coupled Degradation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA produced by laser cladding in which in situ formed TiB2 particles exist in a range of morphologies from well‐dispersed fine particles to locally agglomerated/coarse clusters.
hypotheses.intervention: Control and intentionally modify processing parameters (e.g., slight increases in boron content or adjustment of laser parameters) that promote TiB2 agglomeration, thereby altering their dispersion within the dendritic (DR) region.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (e.g., >300°C) where oxidation kinetics and mechanical abrasion are both activated.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The morphology and spatial distribution of TiB2 reinforcements and the resulting continuity or disruption of the passive oxide film along phase boundaries.
hypotheses.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the TiB2 coarse agglomerates create local stress concentrations and surface irregularities that disrupt the formation and adherence of the protective oxide film. When wear processes mechanically remove portions of an already heterogeneous oxide layer, these agglomerated regions become preferential sites for localized oxidation and enhanced galvanic attack. The mismatch between the bulky TiB2 clusters and the softer matrix exacerbates stress intensity during sliding, further promoting film spallation and accelerating overall degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy with a well‐dispersed, fine TiB2 distribution, the alloy engineered to have more agglomerated/coarse TiB2 is expected to exhibit higher wear rates and increased corrosion current densities—resulting in a higher total degradation rate. Improvement or degradation is measurable in both wear track damage (increased wear depth and width) and electrochemical corrosion parameters (higher icorr and lower passive film resistance), with an anticipated effect on the order of a moderate increase (>20–30% more degradation) subject to experimental quantification.
hypotheses.baseline: The same multi-phase eutectic HEA with fine, uniformly dispersed TiB2 particles which form a relatively continuous passive film under similar elevated temperature wear–corrosion conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is significant only when the operating temperature sufficiently accelerates oxidation kinetics and the wear conditions mechanically stress the heterogeneous oxide film; under milder conditions the effect may be negligible.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of TiB2 agglomeration on degradation rates requires investigation, and the trade-off between particle size and beneficial reinforcement (at lower temperatures) versus detrimental effects (at elevated temperatures) remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic HEA samples via laser cladding that differ primarily in the distribution of TiB2: one with a controlled fine dispersion and one with intentionally agglomerated/coarse TiB2 (achieved via slight processing changes or higher boron levels). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature wear–corrosion tests (e.g., 350°C in a corrosive medium under steady sliding wear).
measurements: Characterization of TiB2 size distribution and dispersion via SEM/EDS.
Wear rate and damage assessment (wear track profiling).
Electrochemical corrosion tests (icorr, Rct, EIS measurements) with mapping of passive film integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with agglomerated TiB2 do not show statistically significant higher wear rates, lower passive film resistance, and increased corrosion current density than the finely dispersed control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s findings on the role of in situ formed TiB2 particles influencing wear and corrosion, extending the concept by linking TiB2 morphology (coarse agglomeration) at elevated temperature to passive film disruption under coupled degradation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes that not only the presence but the size and distribution of TiB2 particles are critical at elevated temperatures; coarse TiB2 agglomerates act as focal points for passive film failure, a mechanistic detail not addressed in the original work.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Differential Oxide Growth at Dendritic–Interdendritic Interfaces Accelerates Degradation via Enhanced Galvanic Coupling.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA with distinct dendritic (DR) and interdendritic (IR) regions that naturally form different passive oxide layers due to compositional variations.
hypotheses.intervention: Leverage the intrinsic differences by operating under elevated temperature conditions to promote differential oxide growth; no compositional modification is introduced but the condition (temperature) is tuned to exaggerate oxide layer heterogeneity.
hypotheses.conditions: Simultaneous exposure to wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (>300°C) where oxidation is accelerated and mechanical wear can selectively remove less-protective oxide regions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The heterogeneous passive films formed at the DR–IR interfaces, where the differences in oxide composition and thickness create localized sites of weakness.
hypotheses.mechanism: Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation and promotes the formation of passive films that differ in composition and adhesion on the dendritic versus interdendritic areas. Mechanical wear then preferentially removes the thinner or less adherent oxide in one region, exposing underlying phases with differing electrochemical potentials. This leads to strong galvanic coupling at the phase boundaries where the oxide is disrupted, thereby locally accelerating corrosion that feeds back into increased wear. The synergy between nonuniform oxide formation and selective film removal under wear conditions leads to accelerated coupled degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline tested at a lower temperature (with more uniform oxide films), the HEA under elevated temperature is expected to show a significant increase in total degradation. Specifically, higher corrosion current density and increased wear damage (deeper and wider wear tracks) are predicted, though the precise magnitude depends on the degree of oxide heterogeneity.
hypotheses.baseline: The same eutectic HEA operating under conditions where the oxide film forms more uniformly (e.g., lower temperature or under static conditions), resulting in a more homogeneous passive layer that better resists wear-corrosion coupling.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant when temperature is high enough to drive significantly different oxidation kinetics in the two regions and when wear stress can externally remove the weaker oxide portions; under isothermal or low-stress conditions the effect may be reduced.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact relative contributions of differential oxide formation and mechanical wear in driving galvanic coupling are not yet well quantified, making precise predictions of degradation rates uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of the multi-phase eutectic HEA and expose them to high-temperature (e.g., 350°C) simultaneous wear–corrosion tests versus a matched set at a lower temperature. Use surface imaging (SEM/EDS) to map oxide film uniformity across dendritic vs interdendritic regions and conduct localized electrochemical measurements along with wear track profilometry.
measurements: Mapping of oxide film thickness and composition across DR and IR regions.
Electrochemical tests (icorr, EIS) taken from micro-regions.
Wear track characterization (depth and morphology).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If elevated temperature does not induce significant oxide layer heterogeneity at the DR–IR interfaces, or if the increased heterogeneity does not correlate with a measurable increase in galvanic corrosion and wear damage compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the understanding from the paper that different microstructural regions play distinct roles in wear and corrosion, combined with general principles of high-temperature oxidation and galvanic coupling from corrosion science.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely integrates the effect of differential oxide growth at inherent microstructural interfaces (dendritic vs interdendritic) and shows how their interaction under elevated temperatures accelerates degradation through localized galvanic effects—a mechanistic detail not previously considered in the paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Oxidation‐Induced Phase Transformation in Interdendritic Regions Triggers Localized Softening and Accelerated Wear–Corrosion.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA comprising a dendritic region enriched in certain elements and an interdendritic region containing Mo-rich σ phases and other intermetallics.
hypotheses.intervention: Exploit the operating condition by subjecting the HEA to elevated temperatures that drive oxidation-induced phase transformation specifically in the interdendritic regions without altering the initial composition.
hypotheses.conditions: Operating under simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (>300°C) where oxidation kinetics are high and can induce phase transformation or degradation of the interdendritic σ phase.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The integrity and phase composition of the interdendritic regions; specifically, the oxidation-induced transformation of Mo-rich σ phases into less protective, porous oxides.
hypotheses.mechanism: At high temperatures, the interdendritic regions experience rapid oxidation which drives partial transformation of stable Mo-rich σ phases into more porous, less adherent oxide products. This phase transformation softens the interdendritic areas, making them more susceptible to mechanical wear. Concurrently, the newly formed porous oxides are less effective as protective barriers, leading to further corrosion. The mutual reinforcement of these processes—wear exposing fresh material that oxidizes even more rapidly, and corrosion weakening the structure against wear—results in an accelerated overall degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy (or the same alloy operated at lower temperature) that maintains its original phase stability, the sample experiencing oxidation-induced phase transformation in the interdendritic regions is expected to show an increased wear rate (deeper, broader wear tracks) and higher corrosion current density. The overall degradation should accelerate appreciably, although the quantitative change remains to be experimentally determined.
hypotheses.baseline: A multi-phase eutectic HEA whose phase composition remains largely stable (with minimal oxidation-induced transformation) under less aggressive (lower temperature) or static conditions, leading to a more robust passive film and lower degradation rates.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism becomes dominant when operating temperatures are high enough to trigger oxidation-induced phase transformations and where cyclic wear continuously exposes the transformed, weakened areas; under isothermal or rapid passivation conditions the effect may diminish.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The extent to which the interdendritic σ phase transforms and how this affects local mechanical properties is not fully quantified, so the magnitude of degradation rate increase is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HEA samples and subject them to elevated temperature wear–corrosion tests while using XRD and microstructural imaging (SEM/TEM) to monitor any phase transformation in the interdendritic regions. Compare these with control samples tested under lower temperature or static conditions.
measurements: Phase analysis pre- and post-test (XRD, microscopy) to detect any oxidation‐induced transformation in interdendritic areas.
Quantitative wear track assessment (depth, width, and morphology).
Electrochemical measurements (icorr, impedance) to assess corrosion performance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no observable oxidation-induced phase transformation in the interdendritic regions or if the transformed regions do not correlate with increased wear and corrosion degradation compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.
