pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The finding in the paper that the σ phase enhances hardness but also induces galvanic corrosion effects (PMC12156342::web::006::1_introduction; PMC12156342::web::007::1_introduction) and the known protective role of oxide films in high-temperature corrosion (TXT::wikipedia::High-temperature_corrosion::014).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis explicitly links the mechanical removal of an evolving oxide film with enhanced galvanic coupling between phases, proposing a control through microstructural homogenization—a route not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: The accelerated coupled degradation arises from a wear-induced breakdown of a transient protective oxide film on the multi-phase eutectic HEA, where the inherent galvanic coupling between the hard, Mo-rich σ phase and the softer, FCC matrix intensifies local anodic dissolution. Repeated mechanical removal of the oxide exposes fresh interfaces with potential differences, which in turn accelerate corrosion and further impair the wear resistance.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix and dispersed Mo-rich σ phases that naturally form galvanic microcells.
fields.intervention: Prepare two alloy variants: one with the standard microstructural heterogeneity and another with a modified heat treatment designed to reduce the potential difference between the σ and FCC phases (e.g., by promoting homogenization of element distribution).
fields.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., > 600 °C) environment under simultaneous wear (reciprocating sliding) and corrosive exposure (chloride-containing electrolyte or controlled oxidizing atmosphere).
fields.structural_mediator: The interphase boundaries between the σ phase and FCC matrix that act as galvanic couples and the integrity of the protective oxide film.
fields.mechanism: Under high-temperature tribocorrosion, mechanical wear repeatedly ruptures the initially forming protective oxide layer. This exposes the underlying phases with distinct electrochemical potentials. The σ phase (being more noble due to Mo enrichment) and the FCC phase form galvanic cells, accelerating anodic dissolution in the FCC regions. The local corrosion further undermines the oxide reformation, infecting the wear interface with pitting and accelerating overall material loss. The cycle of oxide removal, local galvanic corrosion and wear leads to a synergistically increased degradation rate.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the homogenized variant, the standard heterogeneous microstructure will exhibit a significantly higher total degradation, with markedly increased wear volume (potentially on the order of several times that of the baseline) and elevated corrosion current density. The modified alloy with reduced potential differences should show a lower wear-corrosion synergy.
fields.baseline: The untreated multi-phase eutectic HEA with its natural galvanic potential difference and corresponding coupled wear-corrosion degradation.
fields.boundary: Elevated operating temperatures, where a protective oxide film would typically form, and environments that facilitate both mechanical abrasion and corrosive attack.
fields.uncertainty: The exact amplification factor of the degradation rates is uncertain due to possible variations in oxide film kinetics and local potential differences; however, the trend of increased degradation for the heterogeneous case is expected.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct accelerated wear–corrosion tests at elevated temperatures on two sets of samples: one with the standard HEA microstructure and one with a post-heat-treatment homogenized microstructure designed to minimize phase potential differences. Monitor both the wear volume and the corrosion current (using electrochemical measurements) over time.
measurements: Wear volume via white-light interferometry
Corrosion current density via potentiodynamic polarization
Surface oxide integrity via SEM/EDS mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized alloy (with reduced interphase potential differences) does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in coupled degradation—i.e., similar wear and corrosion rates as the standard alloy—the hypothesis that galvanic coupling from oxide film breakdown is the primary accelerator is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: The observed formation of microcracks and poor interfacial integrity at high laser power attributed to thermal stresses (PMC12156342::web::016::3_1_phase_composition_and_microstructure) combined with principles of thermally induced fatigue in multiphase materials (TXT::wikipedia::High-temperature_corrosion::014).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces cyclic thermal expansion mismatch as a key driver of microcracking and coupled degradation in a multi-phase HEA under wear – a mechanism distinct from purely galvanic or compositional change effects discussed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation is driven by thermomechanical fatigue arising from cyclic thermal expansion mismatch between the FCC and σ phases under elevated temperature, which is further amplified by wear; the cyclic stress causes microcracking and spallation at phase boundaries, thereby exposing fresh surfaces to aggressive corrosion, and the resulting pits act as stress concentrators that enhance wear.
fields.material_initial_state: A multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy with inherently different coefficients of thermal expansion between the FCC matrix and the harder σ phase.
fields.intervention: Design a controlled study that adjusts the residual thermal stresses via a post-deposition heat treatment (e.g., a subcritical anneal) aimed at reducing the thermal mismatch between phases. Compare the mechanically polished as-clad HEA with the post-treated HEA.
fields.conditions: Exposure to high temperatures (e.g., 600–700 °C) and cyclic thermal loading combined with continuous sliding wear in a corrosive environment, conditions under which differential thermal expansion becomes significant.
fields.structural_mediator: The phase boundaries between the FCC and σ phases and the residual interlayer stresses built during rapid processing.
fields.mechanism: Under cyclic heating (or sustained elevated temperature coupled with mechanical frictional heating), the mismatch in thermal expansion between the FCC and σ phases generates cyclic stresses at their interfaces. These stresses initiate microcracks along the phase boundaries. The concurrent wear process then exacerbates these microcracks by mechanically removing loosely attached fragments. The microcracks expose fresh metal to the corrosive environment, leading to accelerated corrosion (especially galvanic in nature given the phase differences). The cumulative effect of microcracking, wear-induced spallation, and accelerated localized corrosion results in coupled degradation that is significantly more rapid than the sum of the individual effects.
fields.predicted_outcome: The as-clad alloys with higher residual thermal stresses and pronounced thermal expansion mismatch will show a higher degradation rate, with increased microcrack density, spallation, and higher corrosion currents compared to the post-heat-treated, stress-relieved samples. Total degradation is predicted to increase notably (potentially >2×) in the high-stress samples.
fields.baseline: The untreated, as-clad HEA with its inherent residual stresses and thermal expansion mismatch between phases.
fields.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions of elevated temperature and cyclic thermal/mechanical loading where differential thermal expansion is pronounced; not applicable at room temperature or under static conditions.
fields.uncertainty: Quantitative measures of the degradation amplification due to thermal expansion mismatches are difficult to precisely predict; the directional trend (increased degradation with higher stress) is robust but the exact factor is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one as-clad (with high residual thermal stresses) and one subjected to a subcritical annealing to relieve thermal stresses. Subject both to cyclic elevated temperature wear–corrosion tests and use non-destructive evaluation (e.g., acoustic emission, micro-CT) to monitor microcrack development along with standard wear and corrosion measurements.
measurements: Residual stress measurement via X-ray diffraction
Microcrack density using acoustic emission or micro-CT
Wear volume and corrosion current density measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the stress-relieved samples do not display a statistically lower microcrack density, wear rate, and corrosion rate compared to the as-clad samples under the same test conditions, the hypothesis that cyclic thermal expansion mismatch is driving the accelerated degradation is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: The paper's demonstration of the eutectic HEA's excellent high-temperature stability and the role of the lamellar microstructure, extended here by considering the stability of the oxide films under coupled mechanical and corrosive attack.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the idea that the cyclic disruption of incipient oxide films by wear is the primary driver of accelerated degradation—a mechanism not discussed in the paper—and proposes a passivation treatment as a controlled variable to test its validity.

fields.hypothesis: At elevated temperature, the protective oxide films that normally form on the eutectic HEA are continuously disrupted by mechanical wear, leading to repeated exposure of fresh, unoxidized metal surfaces that corrode rapidly. This cyclic breakdown of the nascent oxide layers accelerates the overall degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion.
fields.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure as produced by conventional casting.
fields.intervention: Introduce a pre-oxidation passivation treatment to create a more robust, adherent oxide layer before exposure to simultaneous wear and corrosion.
fields.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (600–700°C) in an oxidizing atmosphere under sliding (tribocorrosion) conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: The interphase boundaries where thin, nascent oxide films form and are subsequently disrupted.
fields.mechanism: Under high temperatures, each phase develops its own oxide film. However, due to differences in oxidation kinetics between the soft fcc and hard B2 phases, the interface oxide is inherently fragile. When mechanical wear acts on the surface, this film is repeatedly spalled off, exposing fresh metal that rapidly corrodes. The combined process yields accelerated degradation due to the synergy between wear-induced mechanical disruption and corrosive re-oxidation.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the untreated alloy will show an increased overall degradation with both higher abrasive wear (due to lack of lubrication by the oxide film) and more pronounced corrosion attack (due to continuous exposure of fresh metal). Introducing a stable passivating oxide layer should reduce the total degradation (both wear and corrosion) by inhibiting the cyclic film breakdown.
fields.baseline: As-cast eutectic HEA without any pre-oxidation or passivating treatment.

pool.label: C14
pool.builds_on: the paper’s findings on the role of in situ formed TiB2 particles influencing wear and corrosion, extending the concept by linking TiB2 morphology (coarse agglomeration) at elevated temperature to passive film disruption under coupled degradation.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes that not only the presence but the size and distribution of TiB2 particles are critical at elevated temperatures; coarse TiB2 agglomerates act as focal points for passive film failure, a mechanistic detail not addressed in the original work.

fields.hypothesis: TiB2 Agglomeration‐Induced Passive Film Disruption Accelerates Coupled Degradation.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA produced by laser cladding in which in situ formed TiB2 particles exist in a range of morphologies from well‐dispersed fine particles to locally agglomerated/coarse clusters.
fields.intervention: Control and intentionally modify processing parameters (e.g., slight increases in boron content or adjustment of laser parameters) that promote TiB2 agglomeration, thereby altering their dispersion within the dendritic (DR) region.
fields.conditions: Exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (e.g., >300°C) where oxidation kinetics and mechanical abrasion are both activated.
fields.structural_mediator: The morphology and spatial distribution of TiB2 reinforcements and the resulting continuity or disruption of the passive oxide film along phase boundaries.
fields.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the TiB2 coarse agglomerates create local stress concentrations and surface irregularities that disrupt the formation and adherence of the protective oxide film. When wear processes mechanically remove portions of an already heterogeneous oxide layer, these agglomerated regions become preferential sites for localized oxidation and enhanced galvanic attack. The mismatch between the bulky TiB2 clusters and the softer matrix exacerbates stress intensity during sliding, further promoting film spallation and accelerating overall degradation.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy with a well‐dispersed, fine TiB2 distribution, the alloy engineered to have more agglomerated/coarse TiB2 is expected to exhibit higher wear rates and increased corrosion current densities—resulting in a higher total degradation rate. Improvement or degradation is measurable in both wear track damage (increased wear depth and width) and electrochemical corrosion parameters (higher icorr and lower passive film resistance), with an anticipated effect on the order of a moderate increase (>20–30% more degradation) subject to experimental quantification.
fields.baseline: The same multi-phase eutectic HEA with fine, uniformly dispersed TiB2 particles which form a relatively continuous passive film under similar elevated temperature wear–corrosion conditions.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is significant only when the operating temperature sufficiently accelerates oxidation kinetics and the wear conditions mechanically stress the heterogeneous oxide film; under milder conditions the effect may be negligible.
fields.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of TiB2 agglomeration on degradation rates requires investigation, and the trade-off between particle size and beneficial reinforcement (at lower temperatures) versus detrimental effects (at elevated temperatures) remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic HEA samples via laser cladding that differ primarily in the distribution of TiB2: one with a controlled fine dispersion and one with intentionally agglomerated/coarse TiB2 (achieved via slight processing changes or higher boron levels). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature wear–corrosion tests (e.g., 350°C in a corrosive medium under steady sliding wear).
measurements: Characterization of TiB2 size distribution and dispersion via SEM/EDS.
Wear rate and damage assessment (wear track profiling).
Electrochemical corrosion tests (icorr, Rct, EIS measurements) with mapping of passive film integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with agglomerated TiB2 do not show statistically significant higher wear rates, lower passive film resistance, and increased corrosion current density than the finely dispersed control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C15
pool.builds_on: the understanding from the paper that different microstructural regions play distinct roles in wear and corrosion, combined with general principles of high-temperature oxidation and galvanic coupling from corrosion science.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely integrates the effect of differential oxide growth at inherent microstructural interfaces (dendritic vs interdendritic) and shows how their interaction under elevated temperatures accelerates degradation through localized galvanic effects—a mechanistic detail not previously considered in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Differential Oxide Growth at Dendritic–Interdendritic Interfaces Accelerates Degradation via Enhanced Galvanic Coupling.
fields.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA with distinct dendritic (DR) and interdendritic (IR) regions that naturally form different passive oxide layers due to compositional variations.
fields.intervention: Leverage the intrinsic differences by operating under elevated temperature conditions to promote differential oxide growth; no compositional modification is introduced but the condition (temperature) is tuned to exaggerate oxide layer heterogeneity.
fields.conditions: Simultaneous exposure to wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (>300°C) where oxidation is accelerated and mechanical wear can selectively remove less-protective oxide regions.
fields.structural_mediator: The heterogeneous passive films formed at the DR–IR interfaces, where the differences in oxide composition and thickness create localized sites of weakness.
fields.mechanism: Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation and promotes the formation of passive films that differ in composition and adhesion on the dendritic versus interdendritic areas. Mechanical wear then preferentially removes the thinner or less adherent oxide in one region, exposing underlying phases with differing electrochemical potentials. This leads to strong galvanic coupling at the phase boundaries where the oxide is disrupted, thereby locally accelerating corrosion that feeds back into increased wear. The synergy between nonuniform oxide formation and selective film removal under wear conditions leads to accelerated coupled degradation.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline tested at a lower temperature (with more uniform oxide films), the HEA under elevated temperature is expected to show a significant increase in total degradation. Specifically, higher corrosion current density and increased wear damage (deeper and wider wear tracks) are predicted, though the precise magnitude depends on the degree of oxide heterogeneity.
fields.baseline: The same eutectic HEA operating under conditions where the oxide film forms more uniformly (e.g., lower temperature or under static conditions), resulting in a more homogeneous passive layer that better resists wear-corrosion coupling.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant when temperature is high enough to drive significantly different oxidation kinetics in the two regions and when wear stress can externally remove the weaker oxide portions; under isothermal or low-stress conditions the effect may be reduced.
fields.uncertainty: The exact relative contributions of differential oxide formation and mechanical wear in driving galvanic coupling are not yet well quantified, making precise predictions of degradation rates uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of the multi-phase eutectic HEA and expose them to high-temperature (e.g., 350°C) simultaneous wear–corrosion tests versus a matched set at a lower temperature. Use surface imaging (SEM/EDS) to map oxide film uniformity across dendritic vs interdendritic regions and conduct localized electrochemical measurements along with wear track profilometry.
measurements: Mapping of oxide film thickness and composition across DR and IR regions.
Electrochemical tests (icorr, EIS) taken from micro-regions.
Wear track characterization (depth and morphology).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If elevated temperature does not induce significant oxide layer heterogeneity at the DR–IR interfaces, or if the increased heterogeneity does not correlate with a measurable increase in galvanic corrosion and wear damage compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C3
top3.builds_on: The paper's demonstration of the eutectic HEA's excellent high-temperature stability and the role of the lamellar microstructure, extended here by considering the stability of the oxide films under coupled mechanical and corrosive attack.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the idea that the cyclic disruption of incipient oxide films by wear is the primary driver of accelerated degradation—a mechanism not discussed in the paper—and proposes a passivation treatment as a controlled variable to test its validity.

fields.hypothesis: At elevated temperature, the protective oxide films that normally form on the eutectic HEA are continuously disrupted by mechanical wear, leading to repeated exposure of fresh, unoxidized metal surfaces that corrode rapidly. This cyclic breakdown of the nascent oxide layers accelerates the overall degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion.
fields.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure as produced by conventional casting.
fields.intervention: Introduce a pre-oxidation passivation treatment to create a more robust, adherent oxide layer before exposure to simultaneous wear and corrosion.
fields.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (600–700°C) in an oxidizing atmosphere under sliding (tribocorrosion) conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: The interphase boundaries where thin, nascent oxide films form and are subsequently disrupted.
fields.mechanism: Under high temperatures, each phase develops its own oxide film. However, due to differences in oxidation kinetics between the soft fcc and hard B2 phases, the interface oxide is inherently fragile. When mechanical wear acts on the surface, this film is repeatedly spalled off, exposing fresh metal that rapidly corrodes. The combined process yields accelerated degradation due to the synergy between wear-induced mechanical disruption and corrosive re-oxidation.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the untreated alloy will show an increased overall degradation with both higher abrasive wear (due to lack of lubrication by the oxide film) and more pronounced corrosion attack (due to continuous exposure of fresh metal). Introducing a stable passivating oxide layer should reduce the total degradation (both wear and corrosion) by inhibiting the cyclic film breakdown.
fields.baseline: As-cast eutectic HEA without any pre-oxidation or passivating treatment.
fields.boundary: Sustained high temperatures (600–700°C), an oxidizing atmosphere, and applied sliding wear forces representative of relevant service conditions.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in degradation from the pre-passivation treatment is uncertain due to limited characterization of high-temperature oxide film kinetics on such dual-phase materials.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the eutectic HEA samples: one set undergoes a controlled pre-oxidation passivation treatment to form a continuous oxide film, and the other set is left in the as-cast state. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature tribocorrosion tests (e.g., sliding wear in an oxidizing environment at 700°C) and measure weight loss, friction coefficients, and oxide layer integrity.
measurements: Weight loss over time
Surface morphology and oxide film continuity (via SEM/EDS)
Friction coefficient and wear track profile
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passivated samples do not exhibit at least a 10% reduction in overall degradation (both wear and corrosion metrics) compared to the untreated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C12
top3.builds_on: The finding that dual structural‐compositional heterogeneities lead to many interfaces (PMC6687781::web::015::discussion) is extended here by linking those interfaces to differences in oxide formation and spallation under wear–corrosion conditions.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the concept that nonuniform oxide film formation—driven by differences in local diffusion kinetics—creates a dynamic regime where repeated breakdown and reformation of protective films accelerate degradation, a mechanism not considered in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Differential Oxide Film Formation and Spallation Drives Accelerated Degradation.
fields.material_initial_state: A multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring dual structural‐compositional heterogeneities; coarse, well-ordered lamellar regions (ordered L12 and B2) coexist with nanocrystalline regions with higher diffusivity and variable composition.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment at an intermediate temperature that forms a uniform, adherent oxide layer on both regions without significantly altering the bulk microstructure.
fields.conditions: Simultaneous wear and corrosive exposure at elevated temperature where transient oxide films are normally disrupted mechanically.
fields.structural_mediator: The interface between lamellar and nanocrystalline regions where oxide films differ in thickness, adhesion, and composition.
fields.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the rapid diffusion in nanocrystalline zones leads to fast but nonuniform oxide formation that produces a thicker, poorly adherent oxide than the lamellar regions, where slower oxidation yields a thinner, more protective film. During wear, the mechanical removal of these disparate oxides results in repeated breakdown and repair cycles. The mismatch in oxide quality at interfaces causes stress concentration and spallation of the oxide film, thereby exposing fresh metal surfaces to accelerated corrosive attack. This alternation between wear-induced oxide removal and rapid, nonprotective re-oxidation is hypothesized to couple wear and corrosion, enhancing overall degradation.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy that forms heterogeneous oxides naturally, the pre-oxidized sample should exhibit a more uniform and adherent oxide film, leading to lower corrosion pit densities and reduced overall degradation (with similar wear rates but a measurable decrease in corrosion-driven mass loss).
fields.baseline: The as-processed dual heterogeneous alloy, in which oxide formation is dictated by the intrinsic differences in diffusion kinetics between lamellar and nanocrystalline regions.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate when the operating temperature is high enough to induce rapid oxidation (yet below temperatures causing bulk microstructural changes) and when mechanical wear repeatedly disrupts the naturally forming, mismatched oxide films.
fields.uncertainty: The precise differences in oxide film properties between the phases and the quantitative improvement achievable with pre-oxidation treatment remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set following the regular processing route and another subjected to a pre-oxidation heat treatment designed to form a uniform oxide layer. Expose both sets to simultaneous wear and corrosive conditions at elevated temperature. Characterize the oxide film uniformity via surface analytical techniques (such as XPS and TEM cross-sections) and quantify corrosion pit densities and overall mass loss.
measurements: Oxide film thickness and adhesion (via TEM/XPS)
Corrosion pit density and depth (optical/SEM microscopy)
Mass loss during wear–corrosion testing
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess oxide protective quality
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion pit formation and overall degradation compared with untreated samples under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis relating differential oxide film quality to coupled degradation would be refuted.

top3.label: C13
top3.builds_on: This hypothesis leverages the paper's findings on high mechanical heterogeneities and strain partitioning (as seen in the formation of nanocrystalline regions and the associated LAB/GND networks) to explain degradation via defect-enhanced diffusion.
top3.what_is_new: It introduces a mechanism where the accumulation of dislocations at phase boundaries under simultaneous wear and high temperature accelerates diffusive transport of corrosive species, a perspective that connects microstructural mechanics directly to chemical degradation.

fields.hypothesis: Interface-Localized GND Accumulation Enhances Defect-Assisted Diffusive Corrosion.
fields.material_initial_state: A multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy containing sharply contrasting domains—the ordered lamellar regions (L12 and B2) alongside nanocrystalline areas—that inherently generate high densities of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) at the numerous phase boundaries.
fields.intervention: Implement a localized surface mechanical smoothing treatment, such as a mild low-energy shot peening or a controlled surface mechanical attrition process, aimed at reducing initial dislocation pile-up and homogenizing the plastic strain distribution at interfaces.
fields.conditions: Exposure to simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosion at elevated temperature where enhanced dislocation density accelerates defect-assisted diffusion.
fields.structural_mediator: The interfaces between lamellar and nanocrystalline regions that host high GND densities and act as fast diffusion pathways for corrosive species.
fields.mechanism: During wear at elevated temperatures, plastic strain localizes at phase boundaries, generating high GND densities. These accumulated defects enhance the local diffusion of oxygen or aggressive ions along the interfaces. The fast, defect-assisted diffusion promotes accelerated oxidation and corrosion localized at the boundaries. Reducing the initial GND density via a surface smoothing treatment would lessen these diffusion channels, thereby slowing the corrosion rate and decoupling the wear–corrosion interaction.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated specimens, the mechanically resurfaced sample is predicted to show a reduced density of corrosion pits and a lower rate of interfacial oxidation (even if the underlying wear characteristics remain analogous), resulting in a measurable decrease in overall coupled degradation.
fields.baseline: The as-processed alloy with inherent high GND concentrations at its phase boundaries due to strain heterogeneities from hybrid rolling.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is most relevant when elevated temperatures significantly enhance diffusion along defect sites and where the mechanical treatment can effectively reduce localized dislocation pile-ups without altering the overall phase distribution.
fields.uncertainty: Quantifying the exact contribution of GND-driven diffusion to overall corrosion rates and the extent to which mechanical smoothing can reduce these defects introduces uncertainty in the precise degradation reduction achievable.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same alloy: one left as processed and another subjected to the smoothing (surface mechanical attrition) treatment that reduces the density of GNDs at interfaces. Expose both sets to identical simultaneous wear–corrosion tests at elevated temperatures. Map GND density (using electron backscatter diffraction or high-resolution TEM) and quantify local corrosion via pit density and interfacial oxidation depth through microscopy.
measurements: GND density at phase boundaries (EBSD/TEM)
Corrosion pit density and morphology (SEM/optical microscopy)
Electrochemical characterization (EIS, polarization curves)
Wear track profilometry
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the surface-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in GND density and corresponding decrease in localized corrosion relative to untreated samples, then the hypothesis linking GND-facilitated, defect-assisted diffusion to accelerated degradation would be refuted.
